tip: 있으면 (isseumyeon): the -(으)면 (-(eu)myeon) ending means both 'if' and 'when' – here it's 'whenever I'm alone at night', with no separate word for either.
부모님 (bumonim) take 계신 (gyesin) – 계시다 (gyesida) is the respect version of 있다 (itda = to be/stay): for parents and elders, even 'being' somewhere gets the polite verb.
답답해요 (dapdaphaeyo) covers stuffy rooms and stuck conversations alike – talk that's 안 통해서 (an tonghaeseo), not getting through, takes the same word.
놀랐어요 (nollasseoyo) needs no 'was' – 놀라다 (nollada) already means 'get startled', so Korean skips the passive English uses in 'I was startled'.
사람에게 (saramege): you're disappointed 'to' someone in Korean – 에게 (ege) marks the person who let you down, where English reaches for 'by' or 'in'.
눈물이 날 만큼 (nunmuri nal mankeum) = 'to the extent tears come out' – 만큼 (mankeum) follows a whole clause and turns it into 'enough to', measure before the feeling.
것 같아요 (geot gatayo) softens a claim into 'I think' or 'it seems'.
올 것 같아요 (ol geot gatayo): the -ㄹ (-l) on 올 marks a guess about the future – rain that hasn't come yet. A guess about the past switches to -ㄴ/은 (-n/eun).
A noun can't guess on its own – it needs the linking 인 (in): 사람인 것 같아요 (saramin geot gatayo) = 'seems to be a (good) person'. Verbs and adjectives skip that link.
Korean negates inside the guess: 아닌 것 같아요 (anin geot gatayo) is 'seems to not be true', where English pulls the no forward into 'I don't think it's true'.
한국 사람인 것 같아요 (hanguk saramin geot gatayo): a noun needs 인 (in) as the link before the guess – without it, 사람 (saram) can't connect to 'seems to be'.
그래요? (geuraeyo) turns into a question by rising tone alone – the statement uses the exact same words. Korean never flips word order to ask.
The -죠 (-jyo) ending turns a statement into a nudge for agreement – 그렇죠 (geureochyo) is 'that's so, right?'. Drop it and you're just stating a fact.
춥네요 (chumneyo) – the -네요 (-neyo) ending adds 'I just noticed': you felt the cold right now. Plain 추워요 (chuwoyo) would state a bare fact.
할게요 (halgeyo) is not a plain future – the -(으)ㄹ게요 (-lgeyo) ending promises the listener: 'I'll do it, count on it'. A neutral guess would use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-l geoyeyo) instead.
그렇군요 (geureokunyo) carries the -군요 (-gunyo) ending, which flags information you just took in – an out-loud 'oh, I see'. Without it, 그래요 (geuraeyo) is flat agreement.
제 (je) is the humble 'my'. With friends you'd say 내 생각 (nae saenggak); 제 생각에는 (je saenggageneun) keeps the opinion polite from the very first word.
의견에 (uigyeone): 반대 (bandae = opposition) takes the particle 에 (e) – you object 'to' the opinion. Agreeing with 찬성 (chanseong) uses the same 에.
글쎄요 (geulsseyo) buys time politely – and it's often a soft no in disguise. When a Korean answer starts with 글쎄요, don't count on a yes.
아마 (ama), 'probably', normally needs a guessing ending to match: 아마 그럴 거예요 (ama geureol geoyeyo). The word and the ending agree on uncertainty.
-지 않아요 (-ji anayo) is the long-form 'not': 생각하지 않아요 (saenggakhaji anayo) = I don't think so. More measured than fronting 안 (an) – handy for polite disagreement.
있으세요? (isseuseyo) asks about the listener politely – the -(으)세요 (-euseyo) ending raises the person you're asking about.
One-word reactions still carry politeness: 요 (yo) tacked onto 정말 (jeongmal) gives 정말요? (jeongmallyo) – a polite 'really?'. The bare word alone is for close friends.
보다 (boda) attaches to the thing you compare against: 버스보다 (beoseu-boda) = than the bus. KTX가 (KTX-ga) carries only the subject marker – no 'than' word on it.
보다 (boda) attaches to the thing you compare against, not the winner: 기차보다 빨라요 (gicha-boda ppallayo) = faster than the train. 'Than' comes after its noun in Korean.
더 (deo) is optional with 보다 (boda): 어제보다 (더) 더워요 (eoje-boda deo deowoyo) = hotter than yesterday.
Ages compare with 살 (sal): 두 살 많아요 (du sal manayo) = is two years older.
건강에 좋아요 (geongang-e joayo) = good for your health – the particle 에 (e) points at what something is good (or bad) for. No 'for' word; the particle does it.
딱딱해요 (ttakttakhaeyo), 'hard', doubles its syllable to mimic the feel – Korean texture words often work this way: the sound itself imitates the sensation.
훨씬 커요 (hwolssin keoyo) = far bigger, not just bigger – 훨씬 turns a comparison up to 'by far'. Plain 더 (deo) is a mere 'more'.
